paras: The attempted lynching of Anderson at Danville, Kentucky, took place on a Saturday night, probably August 1, 1885, when a mob went to the Danville jail to hang Anderson, a Black man accused of assaulting Mrs. J. H. Hiatt. The jailer had hidden him, and he was later moved to Harrodsburg and Lexington. The Stanford Semi-Weekly Interior Journal used the failure to condemn mobs.

The Interior Journal had earlier reported what it called the "heinous assault on Mrs. J. H. Hiatt by the negro Anderson." J. H. Hiatt later said he had pursued Anderson all afternoon and would have "made short work of the negro" had he been with the party that captured him.

The Interior Journal put the mob at "probably a hundred strong" and said its plans failed because too many members talked. Forewarned, the jailer moved Anderson to a room in the Court-house and "politely showed the men through the jail" to allay suspicion. That night some of the men also stopped two boys, Addie King and Kenley Tribble, on the pike and tried to pull King from his buggy; he got away.

The next day Anderson was taken to the Harrodsburg jail and then to Lexington. At Stanford the same night, a rumor that the mob also meant to hang three Black youths in the jail there led 25 or 30 "leading colored men" to offer to guard them; Judge Varnon had the prisoners removed instead. No report of a trial for Anderson or of arrests of mob members appears in the coverage.

Only two local items in the Interior Journal, on August 4 and 7, 1885, carried the episode; no wire report or Black-press account was found. The paper called Anderson "the rascal" yet mocked the mob for failing to "keep their counsel" and warned that "it is as much murder for a hundred persons to kill a man as if one alone did it." Citing the attack on King as proof of "the cowardliness of mobs," it added that mob members often "more deserve death than the one they start out to kill."

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Anderson at Danville, Kentucky
bases: A mob set out to hang a jailed Black man accused of assault and failed to find him (A1, A2), an attempted lynching.

A mob 'probably a hundred strong' went to Danville to hang Anderson over an alleged assault, but the jailer had hidden him and he was moved to Harrodsburg and Lexington, so no one was killed (A1, A2); it was an attempted lynching.
Both reports are local items in one Stanford, Ky., paper (A1, A2); no other paper, and no Black-press account, was found.

accounts.label: Stanford local editor
accounts.gist: A mob of about a hundred went to Danville to hang Anderson but failed because too many talked; the jailer had hidden Anderson and showed the men through the jail, and Anderson was moved to Harrodsburg and Lexington.

accounts.label: J. H. Hiatt
accounts.gist: Hiatt complained the paper had not credited his pursuit of Anderson and said he would have 'made short work of the negro' had he been with the captors.

framing.detail: The Interior Journal called the alleged assault 'heinous' and Anderson 'the rascal' while treating the mob's failure with scorn, warning that killing by a hundred is still murder and that mob members often 'more deserve death' than their target.

record_check.dossier: Anderson was in jail but was not taken: the jailer hid him in a Court-house room and the mob left without him
the 'pursuit' was the capture before the mob (Hiatt's); there was no seizure or siege, only a visit to the jail, which the jailer showed the men through
the papers name only Danville; no county is stated in this coverage

record_check.record: omits the jailer's ruse and Anderson's removal
record_check.dossier: the jailer hid Anderson and showed the mob through the jail; Anderson was moved to Harrodsburg and then Lexington

Anderson (no first name given), called 'the negro Anderson'; not harmed

sources.note: Local items: a mob 'probably a hundred strong' went to Danville to hang Anderson, accused of assaulting Mrs. J. H. Hiatt, and failed; Hiatt says he pursued Anderson; the same night a mob was said to intend hanging three Black youths in the Stanford jail, who were moved on Judge Varnon's order.
quotes: The mob which went to Danville to hang Anderson was probably a hundred strong, but the most of them could not keep their counsel and the result was a complete failure of their plans.
On our report of the heinous assault on Mrs. J. H. Hiatt by the negro Anderson, Mr. Hiatt complains that no reference was made to his efforts to secure the rascal.
